name: Lena Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm on a crew building a new line out to the wind farm on the moor above Saltby, so it's a forty-minute drive in the crew bus before we even start. I'm the junior, so I'm usually on the ground rigging the hoists and passing gear up, and when they let me climb I'm still slow on the steel. Before this I worked in a café for six years, so it's still a thrill to be doing something this physical. At night I quiz myself with an AI app on the theory, which is honestly how I passed my certificate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the worst part of the job so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Money and wind. My first-year pay barely covers my room and the bus, and I've got maybe three weeks of savings. And the wind up there can stop work for days, which means no overtime and a thin pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown, honestly, because I like the stuff. I'd still post about using it to study, and I'd tell the crew they were right to roll their eyes at me. Hamid on our crew would never let me forget it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the plan I already had: four years to qualify, then maybe move on to drone inspection or protection work. I use AI every day for little things, so if it just stays a handy helper, that's fine. The job's safe, which is the main thing with my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep studying, keep climbing, get faster on the steel by spring. I'd try to get my hobby drone licence upgraded so I'm the person the crew calls when they need a look at a tower. Save whatever's left after rent, which isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, slightly bored. Like being promised fireworks and getting a sparkler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you actually do with AI every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have it quiz me on clearances and knots on the bus, I use it to make sense of the tower manuals, and I had it build me a budget sheet. Last week it helped me write a complaint to my landlord about the damp. It's like a patient friend who knows a bit about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone on the crew mind that you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hamid calls it my imaginary friend. But he's asked me twice to get it to explain his pay slip, so I think he's coming round.

S0.say: It would be a letdown because she enjoys AI tools; she'd still post about studying with it and admit the crew were right to roll their eyes. Her crewmate Hamid would never let her forget it.
S0.think: Her existing plan carries on: qualify in four years, then perhaps move into drone inspection or protection work. If AI just stays a handy helper that's fine, and the job stays safe, which matters with her bank balance.
S0.do: Keeps studying and aims to get faster on the steel by spring. Upgrades her hobby drone licence so she can survey towers for the crew, and saves whatever is left after rent.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit bored, like being promised fireworks and getting a sparkler.
S0.quote: Like being promised fireworks and getting a sparkler.
S0.fieldNote: She's the rare junior who is excited about AI and uses it constantly, from study quizzes to a landlord complaint. Her calm rests on the job's security, which matters because she has about three weeks of savings. She already sees drones as a career path within line work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to make the job safer and better, if workers get a say. Let drones and robots take the dangerous climbs and give us the training to run them. I'd be pushing for that in the union, and posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. I'm already the one who likes the tech, so if crews need someone who can fly the inspection drone and read the data, I want that seat. The risk is that the company uses it to hire fewer of us, and I'm the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book the commercial drone licence course straight away, it's about eight hundred, which I'd have to put on a payment plan. I'd ask the supervisor to let me shadow the inspection team on my days off. And I'd get the union rep to raise training for everyone, so it's not just the keen ones who get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. Nervous about the money, but it feels like a door opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put the course on a payment plan with three weeks' savings. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know I'd be eating pasta for a few months. But I've done riskier, I left a steady café job for a trainee wage. Sitting still feels riskier to me than eight hundred on a payment plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would struggle with this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hamid, maybe, he's great on the steel but hates screens. I'd want the training to be on paid time and in plain language, so people like him don't get pushed out for being good at the old stuff.

S1.say: This is a chance to make the job safer, letting drones and robots take dangerous climbs while workers get trained to run them. She'd push for that in the union and online.
S1.think: It's good for her as the crew's tech person who wants to fly the inspection drone and read its data. The risk is the company hiring fewer workers, and she's the newest.
S1.do: Books a commercial drone licence course of about eight hundred on a payment plan and asks to shadow the inspection team on days off. Gets the union rep to push for training for everyone.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, nervous about money but seeing a door open.
S1.quote: Sitting still feels riskier to me than eight hundred on a payment plan.
S1.fieldNote: She'd take a real money risk with almost no savings, and justifies it by her past jump from café to trainee. Her progressive streak shows in wanting training for everyone, including colleagues like Hamid who dislike screens. She sees steady disruption as her opportunity rather than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public control, fast, because if a few companies own every robot that can do every job, that's not a future, that's a takeover. I'd want a share of the gains for everyone, some kind of basic income. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm less scared than most but more broke than most. My plan was to be the one who runs the robots, but in two years the robots run themselves too. I'd have no savings and a half-finished apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply straight away to the companies building the line robots for field tech jobs, the people who fix them and drive them out to site. If that meant moving to the city, I'd move, I've got nothing tying me to Saltby but a damp room. I'd cut everything else to the bone and join whatever campaign was fighting for a share of the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a jittery kind. I'd be running on adrenaline rather than despair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. Does the speed change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it a sprint, not a career. I wouldn't bother with long courses, I'd go straight for whoever's hiring humans right now and grab it. With two years, the people who move in the first six months are the ones who get a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine, and that I'm moving, both of which would be half true. My dad drove a forklift until a machine took that, so he'd just nod. He'd probably tell me to keep my boots, because you never know.

S2.say: This needs public control fast, since a few companies owning every robot would be a takeover, and everyone should get a share of the gains through something like a basic income. She'd be loud about it.
S2.think: She's less scared than most but more broke, and her plan to run the robots fails if they run themselves within two years. She'd be left with no savings and a half-finished apprenticeship.
S2.do: Applies immediately for field technician jobs with companies building line robots and moves to the city if needed. Cuts spending to the bone and joins campaigns for a share of the gains.
S2.feel: Anxious and jittery, running on adrenaline rather than despair.
S2.quote: With two years, the people who move in the first six months are the ones who get a seat.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest scenario she moves towards the machines rather than away, aiming for jobs maintaining the robots. Her thin cushion keeps her anxious despite her confidence. Her politics jumps to basic income and public control when the change is total.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan it fairly if we start now. I'd want the unions, the government and the companies in one room working out who trains for what. I'd probably volunteer to help run something at the local branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I can finish my apprenticeship and still get onto the robot side early. I'd have real line experience that the tech people don't, and that might be worth something. I'm not sure it lasts past 2031, though, nobody is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone licence and then a course in robotics maintenance at the college in town, evenings. I'd try to save a bit each month, even fifty, so I could move when the right job came up. And I'd keep a list of every company trialling line robots and ask to visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly in a getting-ready way. It's like packing a bag before a trip somebody else booked for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in year four, just before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopefully working for one of those robot companies as the person who actually knows what a live line feels like. That's my pitch: I can climb, I can fly a drone, and I can talk to the machines. If that's not enough by then, nothing is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure it lasts past 2031. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm thirty-two with good skills in a world where skills don't count for much. That's why I care so much about the share-the-gains stuff. I can't out-run a machine forever, I just want to be in a good place when the music stops.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan fairly if unions, government and companies sit down now to decide who trains for what. She'd volunteer to help run something at the branch.
S3.think: She can finish her apprenticeship and still reach the robot side early, with line experience the tech people lack. She's unsure any of it lasts beyond 2031.
S3.do: Gets the drone licence, then takes an evening robotics maintenance course at the town college. Saves around fifty a month to fund a move and tracks every company trialling line robots.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a getting-ready way, like knowing a storm is three days off.
S3.quote: I can't out-run a machine forever, I just want to be in a good place when the music stops.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her plan a bridge from lineworker to robot technician, with a clear pitch built on combining climbing, drones and tech. She admits adaptability only buys time, which is why she cares about sharing the gains. Her calm comes from having a plan, not from security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to build a fair version of this, and we've got no excuse. Fund the training, give workers shares in the robot fleets, and cut the working week. I'd say all that and I'd vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. I'd be thirty-seven with a decade of line work, drone hours and robot know-how. I'm more worried about whether the country shares it than whether I personally land on my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do exactly what I'd do now: qualify, get the drone licence, start the robotics course slowly. I'd use AI to map out which skills are growing, every few months. I'd get active in the party branch, not just the union, because ten years is enough to change the laws.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. It feels like something I can shape instead of something that happens to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any version of the ten years that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one where everyone relaxes because it's far away, and then in year nine nothing's been done. That's the classic. Ten years only helps if people use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years let you do that two wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actually save, for one thing, and do it properly instead of panicking. I could build my skills one by one and still enjoy climbing on the way. Two years is a sprint, ten is a career I'd get to choose.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty to build a fair version of this: fund training, give workers shares in robot fleets and shorten the working week. She'd say it and vote on it.
S4.think: She'd be fine or better, at thirty-seven with line experience, drone hours and robotics skills. She worries more about whether the country shares the gains than about herself.
S4.do: Qualifies, gets the drone licence and starts the robotics course slowly in the first year. Uses AI every few months to map growing skills and becomes active in a party branch, not just the union.
S4.feel: Calm, because it feels like something she can shape.
S4.quote: Ten years only helps if people use it.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she feels in charge and channels energy into politics as well as skills. Her one fear is collective complacency, not her own fate. Her wish for shares in robot fleets and a shorter week marks her progressive outlook clearly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no money and no time, and adaptable doesn't help much if everything changes at once. What would help is a basic income or something like it to catch people, and paid training while you're still working. Even a few months of rent covered would let someone like me make a smart move instead of a desperate one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want a robot on my crew. I would, for the worst climbs in the ice. I just want it to be our robot, not the reason I'm sent home.

headlineQuote: I just want it to be our robot, not the reason I'm sent home.
portrait: Lena Hansen is a 27-year-old first-year lineworker building a new line to a coastal wind farm, a former café worker who uses AI every day to study, budget and even write to her landlord. She has about three weeks of savings and a first-year wage, but she likes risk and sees drones and robots as her way forward. She's calm through the plateau and steady disruption, anxious but moving fast if AGI comes in two years, and calm again with ten, when she feels she can shape things. Her plans run from a drone licence to robotics maintenance and moving to wherever humans are still hired. Her politics is about public control and sharing the gains, and she'd welcome a robot on the crew as long as workers own it.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because she'd have no money and no time, and being adaptable doesn't help much when everything changes at once.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income or something like it to catch people, and paid training while still working, so people like her can make a smart move instead of a desperate one.
